llm_plan:
## ASSESSMENT
1. **Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), improving on high-dose prednisone**
   - Recent platelet nadir **10K on 01/09/07** with no reported bleeding. Prednisone was increased to **60 mg/day** with subsequent rise in platelets to **43K on 01/16/07**, consistent with steroid-responsive ITP. Petechiae on legs have resolved, supporting clinical improvement. Hematology concurs with beginning a taper now that platelet count has recovered above the most critical range.

## PLAN
1. **ITP / Thrombocytopenia management**
   - **Steroid taper (per hematology):**
     - Decrease prednisone to **40 mg PO daily x 3 days**, then
     - Decrease to **20 mg PO daily** thereafter.
   - **Monitoring / labs:**
     - **CBC with platelet count** in **~1 week** (or sooner if symptoms) to ensure platelets remain stable during taper.
     - Repeat CBC again **1 week later** if platelets are falling or if dose changes are needed.
   - **Bleeding precautions / counseling:**
     - Review signs/symptoms requiring urgent evaluation: new/worsening petechiae/purpura, gum bleeding, epistaxis, heavy menses, hematuria, melena, hematemesis, severe headache/neurologic symptoms.
     - Avoid **NSAIDs/aspirin** and minimize trauma/contact activities while platelets remain low.
   - **When to escalate care:**
     - If platelets fall back toward **<20K** or if any clinically significant bleeding occurs: urgent recheck CBC and coordinate with hematology for consideration of therapy escalation (e.g., higher steroid dose, IVIG, etc., per hematology).

2. **Medication safety while on prednisone**
   - Continue taper as above; take with food.
   - Monitor for steroid adverse effects (hyperglycemia, mood change, insomnia, edema, hypertension, GI irritation). Consider gastric protection if patient has GERD/ulcer history or develops symptoms.

3. **Coordination with hematology**
   - Continue co-management with her hematologist; share upcoming CBC results and clinical status during taper.

4. **Follow-up**
   - **Clinic follow-up in 1–2 weeks** (after next CBC) to review platelet trend and adjust prednisone dose further.
   - Earlier follow-up/ED evaluation immediately for any bleeding symptoms or if patient feels unwell.

presentation: HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:,  Ms. Connor is a 50-year-old female who returns to clinic for a wound check.  The patient underwent an APR secondary to refractory ulcerative colitis.  Subsequently, she developed a wound infection, which has since healed.  On our most recent visit to our clinic, she has her perineal stitches removed and presents today for followup of her perineal wound.  She describes no drainage or erythema from her bottom.  She is having good ostomy output.  She does not describe any fevers, chills, nausea, or vomiting.  The patient does describe some intermittent pain beneath the upper portion of the incision as well as in the right lower quadrant below her ostomy.  She has been taking Percocet for this pain and it does work.  She has since run out has been trying extra strength Tylenol, which will occasionally help this intermittent pain.  She is requesting additional pain medications for this occasional abdominal pain, which she still experiences.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: , Temperature 95.8, pulse 68, blood pressure 132/73, and weight 159 pounds.  This is a pleasant female in no acute distress.  The patient's abdomen is soft, nontender, nondistended with a well-healed midline scar.  There is an ileostomy in the right hemiabdomen, which is pink, patent, productive, and protuberant.  There are no signs of masses or hernias over the patient's abdomen.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: , This is a pleasant 50-year-old female who has undergone an APR secondary to refractory ulcerative colitis.  Overall, her quality of life has significantly improved since she had her APR.  She is functioning well with her ileostomy.  She did have concerns or questions about her diet and we discussed the BRAT diet, which consisted of foods that would slow down the digestive tract such as bananas, rice, toast, cheese, and peanut butter.  I discussed the need to monitor her ileostomy output and preferential amount of daily output is 2 liters or less.  I have counseled her on refraining from soft drinks and fruit drinks.  I have also discussed with her that this diet is moreover a trial and error and that she may try certain foods that did not agree with her ileostomy, however others may and that this is something she will just have to perform trials with over the next several months until she finds what foods that she can and cannot eat with her ileostomy.  She also had questions about her occasional abdominal pain.  I told her that this was probably continue to improve as months went by and I gave her a refill of her Percocet for the continued occasional pain.  I told her that this would the last time I would refill the Percocet and if she has continued pain after she finishes this bottle then she would need to start ibuprofen or Tylenol if she had continued pain.  The patient then brought up some right hand and arm numbness, which has been there postsurgically and was thought to be from positioning during surgery.  This is all primarily gone away except for a little bit of numbness at the tip of the third digit as well as some occasional forearm muscle cramping.  I told her that I felt that this would continue to improve as it has done over the past two months since her surgery.  I told her to continue doing hand exercises as she has been doing and this seems to be working for her.  Overall, I think she has healed from her surgery and is doing very well.  Again, her quality of life is significantly improved.  She is happy with her performance.  We will see her back in six months just for a general routine checkup and see how she is doing at that time.

llm_plan:
## ASSESSMENT
1. **Status post abdominoperineal resection (APR) for refractory ulcerative colitis; prior postoperative wound infection—now resolved.**  
   Perineal wound previously infected and stitches removed at last visit; today she reports **no drainage/erythema** and has **no systemic symptoms** (fever/chills). Exam shows well-healed abdominal incision and no concerning findings.

2. **Intermittent postoperative abdominal/incisional pain (upper incision and RLQ near ostomy), without peritoneal signs or obstructive symptoms.**  
   Pain is intermittent and responsive to Percocet previously; currently no abdominal tenderness, distension, nausea/vomiting, fevers, or ostomy output issues. Differential includes **normal post-surgical healing/neuropathic pain**, abdominal wall strain, adhesions; less likely but important to monitor for **parastomal hernia, abscess, bowel obstruction, or stoma complication** given location near ostomy—none suggested on today’s exam/history.

3. **Ileostomy—functioning well.**  
   Ostomy is pink/patent/productive with good output by report; no evidence of ischemia, retraction, or peristomal complication on exam.

---

## PLAN
1. **Perineal wound / postoperative follow-up**
   - Continue routine wound care and hygiene; keep area clean and dry.
   - No antibiotics indicated today (no signs of infection).
   - Review return precautions: new/worsening drainage, redness, swelling, foul odor, fevers/chills.

2. **Pain management (postoperative intermittent abdominal pain)**
   - **First-line:** Acetaminophen as needed (do not exceed **3,000 mg/day** total from all sources).  
   - **Avoid NSAIDs** unless cleared by her surgical/GI team (ileostomy/dehydration risk and GI considerations).
   - Discussed opioids: given healed wound, benign exam, and intermittent nature, **do not plan to restart Percocet as ongoing therapy**. If pain becomes more frequent/severe or limits function, patient should be re-evaluated rather than managed with repeated opioid refills.
   - Consider **topical lidocaine patch** to focal abdominal wall/incisional discomfort if localized (OTC 4% or Rx 5% depending on availability/tolerance).
   - Encourage gradual activity increase, avoid heavy lifting/straining to reduce abdominal wall pain.

3. **Evaluate for complications if pain persists or worsens**
   - No imaging required today based on reassuring exam and stable symptoms.
   - If pain increases, becomes constant, is associated with decreased ostomy output, vomiting, fevers, or a new bulge near stoma/incision:  
     - Order **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** (and oral contrast per local protocol) to evaluate for abscess, obstruction, hernia, or other postoperative complication.  
     - Check labs: **CBC**, **CMP** (electrolytes/renal function), and **CRP** as clinically indicated.

4. **Ileostomy care / hydration**
   - Continue current ostomy regimen.
   - Emphasize hydration and electrolyte intake; monitor output. Seek care urgently for high-output ileostomy, dizziness, decreased urination, or signs of dehydration.
   - Offer/continue **Wound/Ostomy nurse** follow-up if any pouching issues, skin irritation, or concerns develop.

5. **Follow-up**
   - Routine surgical follow-up in **4–6 weeks** (or sooner if symptoms escalate).
   - **Earlier/urgent return** for: fever, new wound drainage/redness, escalating abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, inability to tolerate PO, reduced ostomy output, or new bulge around the stoma/incision (concern for obstruction or hernia).

## ASSESSMENT
1. **History of lipomyelomeningocele s/p repair x2 (neonatal and age 3.5 yrs), now with new bilateral leg pain – concern for symptomatic retethering of the spinal cord (tethered cord syndrome)**
   - She has a known risk of **retethering** after prior lipomyelomeningocele repairs.
   - Over the last several months she has developed **new, progressive bilateral lateral leg pain (worse at night)** requiring frequent OTC analgesics.
   - She **denies new bowel/bladder dysfunction** and has **no new motor weakness on exam**, which is reassuring, but **pain can be an early symptom** of retethering.
   - Baseline/known **patchy sensory loss L4–S1** noted; exam today shows diminished sensation in this distribution with preserved proprioception, strength, and reflexes.

2. **Bilateral leg pain – differential includes neuropathic/radicular pain related to tethering vs musculoskeletal overuse/orthopedic causes**
   - Distribution and nocturnal worsening raise possibility of neuropathic pain; however, normal strength/reflexes and lack of clear radicular findings mean orthopedic and other causes should also be considered if spinal imaging is unrevealing.

3. **Asthma/allergic disease (on montelukast) – stable by history**
   - Not the focus of today’s visit.

---

## PLAN
1. **Evaluate for retethering / structural cause**
   - **MRI lumbosacral spine** to assess for: low-lying conus/tethering, recurrent lipoma, postoperative scarring, syrinx, and nerve root compression.  
     - Order **MRI lumbar spine without contrast** (contrast only if radiology/neurosurgery feels needed for postoperative scar vs mass characterization).
   - Consider **MRI thoracic spine** (or entire spine) if symptoms, exam, or lumbar MRI suggests syrinx or additional pathology.

2. **Assess for occult neuro-urologic changes (even if asymptomatic)**
   - Obtain **screening urinalysis** and **post-void residual** (bladder scan) as a baseline.
   - If any concern on screening or if MRI suggests retethering, recommend **urology referral for urodynamic testing** to detect early neurogenic bladder changes.

3. **Symptom management while workup is pending**
   - Continue OTC analgesics but **avoid stacking multiple NSAIDs**:
     - Use **ibuprofen OR naproxen** as needed with food; avoid exceeding age/weight-appropriate dosing.
     - **Acetaminophen** may be used as an alternative; avoid exceeding daily maximum dose.
   - Avoid routine use of **Tylenol PM** for pain/sleep; discuss sleep hygiene and safer short-term options if needed.
   - If pain appears neuropathic and persists, consider starting a neuropathic agent (e.g., **gabapentin**) **after imaging review** and discussion with family regarding risks/benefits.

4. **Rehabilitation / activity**
   - **Physical therapy referral** for gentle core/hip strengthening, hamstring/hip flexor stretching, posture mechanics, and activity modification (avoid activities that exacerbate pain until imaging complete).
   - Encourage maintaining light activity as tolerated; avoid prolonged positions that increase symptoms.

5. **Follow-up**
   - **Follow up after MRI** (within ~2–4 weeks or sooner once results are available) to review imaging and decide next steps.
   - If MRI confirms retethering and symptoms correlate, discuss **neurosurgical options** (detethering) including expected benefits/risks and goals (pain control, prevention of neurologic decline).

6. **Return precautions (urgent evaluation)**
   - Go to ED / call urgently for any **new or worsening weakness**, gait deterioration, new numbness, **new bowel or bladder changes** (incontinence, retention, recurrent UTIs), saddle anesthesia, fever with back pain, or rapidly escalating pain.

7. **Asthma**
   - Continue **montelukast** as prescribed; follow with primary care/allergy as usual.

llm_plan:
## ASSESSMENT
1. **Large local reaction to Hymenoptera (yellow jacket) sting – right wrist/hand with edema extending to forearm/elbow.**  
   Presentation is consistent with a **large local allergic reaction** (marked swelling progressing over 24 hours) without systemic symptoms. He denies prior anaphylaxis and currently has **no shortness of breath, throat tightness, wheeze, urticaria, palpitations, or hypotension**. Exam shows swelling with minimal erythema and no tenderness or infectious signs, making cellulitis less likely at this time.

2. **Risk counseling: recurrent large local reactions to wasp stings.**  
   History of similar swelling with prior stings suggests predisposition to large local reactions. Risk of future anaphylaxis is still generally low but not zero; needs education on warning symptoms and prevention.

## PLAN
### Symptomatic treatment (large local reaction)
- **Cold compresses** to hand/forearm 10–15 min at a time, several times daily for next 24–48 hours.
- **Elevation** of the right arm above heart level as much as possible.
- **Oral antihistamine:**  
  - **Cetirizine 10 mg PO daily** (or loratadine 10 mg daily) for 5–7 days.  
  - If itching is significant at night: **diphenhydramine 25–50 mg PO at bedtime PRN** (caution sedation; avoid driving/alcohol).
- **Anti-inflammatory/pain control:**  
  - **Ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO every 6–8 hours PRN** with food (avoid if history of ulcer/renal disease/anticoagulants).  
  - Alternative: acetaminophen as needed.
- **Oral steroid (given extent of swelling):**  
  - **Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x 3 days, then 20 mg PO daily x 2 days** (5-day course). Discussed potential side effects (insomnia, mood changes, elevated glucose, GI upset).  
- **Topical:** hydrocortisone 1% thin layer to sting area 1–2x/day PRN itch (avoid broken skin).

### Monitor for complications / return precautions
- **Go to ED / call 911 immediately** for any systemic symptoms: trouble breathing, wheeze, throat tightness, lip/tongue swelling, generalized hives, vomiting, dizziness/fainting, chest tightness.
- **Call/return urgently** if: rapidly worsening redness/warmth, increasing pain, fever, pus/drainage, red streaking, numbness/tingling, inability to move fingers, or swelling continues to progress beyond 48 hours (concern for secondary infection or compartment-type symptoms—rare).

### Infection considerations
- No current evidence of cellulitis/abscess; **no antibiotics today**. Reassess if erythema, warmth, tenderness, fever, or drainage develops.

### Allergy prevention / future risk
- **Avoidance counseling** (protective clothing outdoors, caution with sweet drinks/garbage, do not disturb nests).
- Discussed that recurrent large local reactions do not automatically mean anaphylaxis, but he should recognize warning signs.
- **Epinephrine autoinjector:** given recurrent significant reactions and concern about “severe reaction,” offer shared decision-making; **prescribe epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM** (two-pack) and review use if any systemic symptoms occur, then call 911. *(If patient declines, document and reinforce precautions.)*
- **Referral:** Offer **Allergy/Immunology** referral for evaluation (venom-specific IgE testing and discussion of venom immunotherapy if systemic reaction ever occurs; may also be considered in selected cases with frequent unavoidable stings).

### Labs / imaging
- **None indicated** today (no systemic symptoms, afebrile, no signs of infection or retained foreign body).

### Follow-up
- **Recheck in 48–72 hours** (clinic/televisit) if not clearly improving, or sooner if worsening.  
- Otherwise routine follow-up with PCP as needed.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Uterine papillary serous carcinoma, s/p TAH/BSO and adjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel (completed 1/18/08), currently without evidence of disease (NED).**  
   - Surveillance CT chest/abdomen/pelvis on 1/28/08 shows no local recurrence or distant metastasis and an unremarkable vaginal cuff. Patient asymptomatic from an oncologic standpoint and pelvic exam today without masses or bleeding.

2. **Peripheral neuropathy, mild, likely chemotherapy-induced (paclitaxel-related), predominantly right upper extremity numbness.**  
   - Stable, non-progressive, no burning/tingling, no lower extremity involvement, and no focal neuro deficits on exam today; will monitor closely. Unilateral predominance warrants reassessment if it progresses or becomes painful.

3. **Elevated blood pressure (143/83) without acute symptoms.**  
   - Mild elevation today; needs confirmation with repeat readings and primary care follow-up to determine if persistent hypertension.

4. **Scalp/skin lesion (“mole”) of several months’ duration.**  
   - Needs direct visualization and dermatologic evaluation to rule out atypical nevus/skin cancer, especially given new/changing lesion history.

5. **Incidental right gonadal vein thrombosis on CT, described as probably chronic; asymptomatic.**  
   - No reported pain, fever, or other symptoms suggestive of acute thrombosis; management depends on chronicity, extent, and risk factors. Requires review of CT details and consideration of further evaluation.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Uterine papillary serous carcinoma – post-treatment surveillance (NED)
- **Surveillance schedule:**  
  - **Follow-up visits every 3 months for the next 2 years**, then space to every 6 months until 5 years, then annually (adjust per institutional protocol).  
  - At each visit: focused ROS, **pelvic exam/speculum exam**.
- **Labs:**  
  - Obtain **CBC and CMP** today or at next visit to establish post-chemo baseline/recovery.  
  - If she had a pre-treatment elevated tumor marker (e.g., **CA-125**), then **trend CA-125** at surveillance visits; if not previously informative, routine use is optional.
- **Imaging:**  
  - No routine imaging required today given recent CT NED; **repeat CT chest/abdomen/pelvis only if symptoms, exam findings, or rising tumor marker** suggest recurrence (or per high-risk surveillance protocol if used in this practice).
- **Counseling:**  
  - Review recurrence symptoms to report promptly: new vaginal bleeding, pelvic/abdominal pain or bloating, early satiety, unexplained weight loss, new cough/SOB, bone pain.

### 2) Neuropathy (likely chemotherapy-induced; unilateral RUE numbness)
- **Monitor** severity and distribution; document at each visit.
- **Evaluate reversible contributors:** consider **TSH, vitamin B12, fasting glucose/A1c** if symptoms persist or progress.
- **Symptomatic treatment:** not needed currently given numbness only and stable; if it becomes painful or function-limiting, consider **gabapentin or duloxetine** and/or **PT/OT**.
- **Return precautions:** worsening, spread to legs, weakness, neck pain/radicular pain, or functional impairment → prompt reassessment; consider neuro exam repeat and **EMG/NCS** or cervical spine evaluation if clinically indicated.

### 3) Elevated blood pressure
- **Repeat BP** in clinic today if possible and ensure proper cuff/positioning.
- Recommend **home BP log** (AM/PM readings for 1–2 weeks).
- **Follow up with primary care** for hypertension diagnosis/management if readings remain ≥130–140 systolic or ≥80–90 diastolic consistently.

### 1) Suspected RIGHT carpal tunnel syndrome
- **Conservative management (first-line):**
  - **Night wrist splint** in **neutral position** (carpal tunnel brace) every night for **4–6 weeks**; can also use during repetitive keyboarding if helpful.
  - **Activity/ergonomic modification:** continue keyboard/desk adjustments; avoid sustained wrist flexion/extension; take frequent micro-breaks; consider wrist pad and proper chair/desk height.
  - **Anti-inflammatory/pain control (if no contraindications):**

    - Consider **topical diclofenac gel** to wrist/hand PRN if prefers topical therapy.
- **When to escalate / further evaluation:**
  - If symptoms **persist beyond 4–6 weeks**, worsen, or if any **weakness, dropping objects, thenar (thumb base) muscle wasting**, or constant numbness develops → proceed with **EMG/NCS** to confirm severity and guide next steps.
  - If moderate/severe or refractory symptoms → discuss **corticosteroid injection** and/or **referral to Hand Surgery/Orthopedics** for further management.

- Use same **NSAID/topical diclofenac** options above as needed.
- If persistent pain, decreased function, or focal joint tenderness at follow-up → consider **right hand/thumb X-ray** and/or referral to hand therapy/orthopedics.

### 3) Elevated blood pressure

- Recommend **home BP monitoring** (arm cuff): record **2 readings AM + 2 readings PM for 7 days** and bring log.
- Lifestyle: limit sodium, increase activity as tolerated, weight reduction.

### Follow-up

- Earlier follow-up if symptoms worsen or any weakness develops.

2. **Possible allergic rhinitis component (periorbital puffiness, congestion).**  
   Puffy eyes and nasal swelling could reflect allergies, though fever/fatigue favor viral illness; may be mixed picture.

3. **History of intermittent elevated blood pressure and recent weight gain.**  
   Not the primary issue today but warrants follow‑up given reported “episodes of high blood pressure” and ~14 lb weight gain over the past year.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Viral URI / sore throat / hoarseness
- **No antibiotics** (testing negative; clinical picture consistent with viral illness).
- **Supportive care:**
  - **Fluids**, rest; warm tea/broth.
  - **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** as needed for throat pain/fever (weight‑based dosing per label/parent guidance).
  - **Salt‑water gargles** 3–4x/day; throat lozenges as needed.
  - **Voice rest**; avoid yelling/whispering (both strain the voice).
- **Nasal care for post‑nasal drip/congestion:**
  - **Saline nasal spray/irrigation** 1–2x/day.
  - Avoid oral decongestants (e.g., pseudoephedrine) given history of elevated BP.

### 2) Suspected allergic rhinitis component
- Prefer a non‑sedating antihistamine over diphenhydramine:
  - **Cetirizine 10 mg PO daily** (or loratadine 10 mg daily) for 1–2 weeks, then PRN.
  - **Stop Benadryl during the day** due to sedation/fatigue.
- If congestion persists: start **fluticasone nasal spray** (OTC) **1 spray each nostril daily** for 2–4 weeks (use consistently for best effect).

### 3) Monitoring / when to reassess
- **Expected course:** Viral symptoms typically improve over **3–7 days**; hoarseness can lag.
- **Return sooner / urgent evaluation** for any of the following:
  - Trouble breathing, drooling, inability to swallow, signs of dehydration
  - Fever **≥ 102°F** or fever lasting **>3 days**
  - Worsening unilateral throat pain, “hot potato” voice, neck swelling/stiffness
  - New eye redness/pain, marked worsening eyelid swelling, or facial swelling
  - Symptoms that **worsen after initial improvement** or persist **>10 days** (concern for bacterial sinusitis or other complication)
- **Follow‑up:** If not clearly improving in **3–5 days**, or sooner if worse.

### 4) Blood pressure / weight

  - **Repeat BP measurements** (proper cuff size; consider home BP log)
  - Nutrition/physical activity counseling and growth/weight trend review
  - Consider screening labs per PCP discretion (commonly: **fasting lipid panel, HbA1c/glucose**, +/- CMP)

## ASSESSMENT
1. **3-week postpartum visit – normal recovery**
   - Breastfeeding without concerns, lochia decreasing appropriately (now yellowish), minimal bleeding, no cramping/clots, uterus involuting on exam. No headache or other concerning symptoms reported.

2. **Allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis / seasonal allergies**
   - Classic symptoms (itchy/watery eyes, rhinorrhea, sneezing) with exam showing clear nasal drainage and watery ocular discharge. Ear “pressure” likely eustachian tube dysfunction related to allergic congestion. No signs of bacterial infection.

3. **Symptomatic external hemorrhoid with intermittent bright red rectal bleeding**
   - Pain with bowel movements and occasional BRBPR; external inflamed hemorrhoid seen on exam; stool guaiac negative and anoscopy without other lesions. Likely postpartum-related hemorrhoid exacerbated by stool consistency/diet.

4. **Medication allergy history**
   - Reports allergy to diphenhydramine (Benadryl) (details unclear), important for antihistamine selection.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Postpartum care
- Reassurance: postpartum course and lochia pattern appear normal for 3 weeks.
- Continue **prenatal vitamins** while breastfeeding.
- Counsel:
  - Return precautions: heavy bleeding (soaking >1 pad/hr), fever/chills, worsening pelvic pain, foul-smelling discharge, severe headache/vision changes, chest pain/SOB, leg swelling/pain, mood concerns.
- Sexual activity: may resume when comfortable; recommend waiting until bleeding resolved and perineal/rectal discomfort improved.
- Contraception: review options compatible with breastfeeding (e.g., condoms now; consider progestin-only pill, implant, IUD at/after routine postpartum visit). Confirm plan at next visit.

### 2) Allergic rhinitis / conjunctivitis (breastfeeding-safe approach)
- **Avoid diphenhydramine** given reported allergy and also due to potential sedation and possible milk supply effects.
- Start:
  - **Intranasal saline** spray/rinse daily and as needed.
  - **Intranasal corticosteroid**: e.g., **fluticasone** 1 spray/nostril daily (may increase to 2 sprays/nostril daily if needed) for congestion/postnasal symptoms.
  - **Non-sedating oral antihistamine**: **loratadine 10 mg PO daily** *or* **cetirizine 10 mg PO daily** (choose one; monitor for infant irritability/sedation though uncommon).
  - For eyes: **ketotifen ophthalmic** 1 drop each eye BID PRN itching/watering (or artificial tears PRN).
- Environmental measures: pollen avoidance (shower after outdoors, keep windows closed, HEPA if available).
- If ear pressure persists >2–3 weeks despite above or develops ear pain/fever/hearing loss, re-evaluate for otitis media/sinusitis.

### 3) External hemorrhoid / rectal bleeding
- Conservative treatment:
  - Increase **dietary fiber** (vegetables, whole grains) and **fluids**.
  - Consider **psyllium** daily (titrate to soft, formed stools).
  - **Stool softener**: **docusate 100 mg** PO 1–2 times daily as needed.
  - **Sitz baths** warm water 10–15 minutes 1–2 times/day and after bowel movements.
  - **Topical hemorrhoid therapy**: e.g., **hydrocortisone 1% cream** thin layer to external hemorrhoid BID for up to 7 days (avoid prolonged use); may add witch hazel pads PRN.
  - Pain control: **acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** as needed if no contraindications.
- Return precautions: increased bleeding, black/tarry stool, dizziness, severe pain, fever, or no improvement within 1–2 weeks.
- If persistent bleeding/pain beyond conservative therapy or recurrent significant bleeding, consider referral to **GI/colorectal** for further evaluation (especially given age).

### 4) Testing / imaging
- No routine labs/imaging needed today based on stable vitals, reassuring postpartum course, and guaiac-negative stool.
- Consider CBC only if bleeding becomes heavier or symptoms of anemia develop.

### 5) Follow-up
- Routine postpartum follow-up at **6 weeks postpartum** (or sooner if symptoms worsen).
- Earlier follow-up in **2–4 weeks** if allergies not controlled with above regimen or hemorrhoid symptoms persist.

## ASSESSMENT
55-year-old African-American male with **new onset seizures** and MRI showing a **right contrast-enhancing temporal mass**. Given the combination of (1) adult-onset seizures, (2) enhancing intra-axial temporal lesion, and (3) concern for aggressive imaging characteristics, the leading diagnosis is **high-grade glioma (e.g., glioblastoma/anaplastic astrocytoma)**. Differential also includes **metastasis**, **primary CNS lymphoma**, and less likely **tumefactive demyelination/abscess** depending on imaging pattern and clinical context. Neurologically intact on exam today (GCS 15, no focal deficits), but lesion location and seizure presentation place him at risk for recurrent seizures and potential mass effect.

## PLAN
### 1) Right temporal enhancing brain mass – highly concerning for high-grade glioma
- **Neurosurgical management**
  - Discussed that tissue diagnosis is required.
  - Plan for **neurosurgical intervention**: **maximal safe resection** if lesion is resectable; otherwise **stereotactic biopsy** for diagnosis.
  - Obtain/confirm imaging for surgical planning (see below).
- **Imaging**
  - **MRI brain w/ and w/o contrast with neuronavigation (stealth) protocol** if not already performed.
  - Consider **MR spectroscopy/perfusion** if diagnostic uncertainty remains.
  - If concern for systemic malignancy or if imaging suggests metastasis: **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast** (or PET/CT per local protocol) after discussion.
- **Pre-op / baseline testing**
  - **CBC, CMP/electrolytes, PT/INR, aPTT, type & screen**.
  - **EKG** and additional pre-anesthesia testing as indicated.
- **Steroids / edema**
  - If symptomatic from mass effect/edema (headache, progressive neuro deficits, significant edema on MRI): start **dexamethasone** (e.g., 4 mg q6h) with GI prophylaxis; however **defer routine steroids** today given normal neuro exam unless imaging/symptoms warrant.
  - If steroids started: consider **PJP prophylaxis** if prolonged high-dose course anticipated per institutional policy.
- **Oncology coordination (post-path)**
  - After pathology: anticipate referral to **Neuro-oncology and Radiation Oncology** for adjuvant therapy planning (e.g., radiation ± temozolomide if high-grade glioma).

### 2) Seizure disorder secondary to brain mass
- **Antiepileptic therapy**
  - Continue current antiseizure medication if already prescribed (verify agent/dose and adherence).
  - If not on therapy or recurrent seizures: initiate **levetiracetam** (typical starting 500 mg BID, adjust for renal function and tolerability) and titrate as needed.
- **Safety / counseling**
  - **No driving**, operating heavy machinery, swimming alone, climbing heights until cleared per state law and neurology recommendations.
  - Seizure precautions reviewed; instruct family on when to call EMS (seizure >5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, injury, new focal deficits).
- **Neurology**
  - **Neurology consult** for seizure management and perioperative AED strategy (including peri-op dosing and duration).

### 3) Follow-up / return precautions
- **Timing**
  - Expedite workup: arrange **neurosurgery follow-up within days** to finalize operative plan.
  - Post-procedure follow-up to review pathology and next steps within **1–2 weeks** (or sooner if inpatient course dictates).
- **Return precautions**
  - Go to ED immediately for worsening headaches, vomiting, confusion, new weakness/numbness, speech/vision changes, fever, or any recurrent/prolonged seizures.

### 4) Documentation / records
- Obtain outside MRI images/report if not already in chart.
- Ensure medication list, seizure history (frequency, last event), and any cancer history/systemic symptoms are documented prior to operative planning.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Erectile dysfunction (ED), mixed features (likely primarily situational/psychogenic vs mild vasculogenic)**
   - 33-year-old male with difficulty achieving/maintaining erections “much less than half the time” by questionnaire, though he describes severity as mild and main concern is “lasting longer.” No GU exam abnormalities, no history of pelvic trauma, testicular infection, hernia, smoking, or significant comorbidities. Mildly decreased desire reported.
   - Given young age and limited medical history, **performance anxiety/stress/sleep disruption** (works 2nd shift, fatigue) is possible, but ED can be an early marker of cardiometabolic disease; needs basic evaluation.
   - Also clarify whether complaint is **premature ejaculation vs ED** (patient’s stated goal is erections “last longer”), though questionnaire suggests erectile maintenance issues.

2. **Borderline elevated diastolic blood pressure (120/90)**
   - Single reading; warrants repeat measurements and risk factor screening.

## PLAN
### ED evaluation / work-up
- **Clarify symptoms**: onset, duration, morning/nocturnal erections, masturbation performance, partner-specific vs generalized, timing (before vs after penetration), ejaculation latency (screen for premature ejaculation), libido, pornography use, relationship stress, depression/anxiety symptoms, sleep quality/shift-work effects.
- **Labs (morning, fasting if possible):**
  - **Total testosterone (8–10 AM)**; if low, repeat and add free testosterone/SHBG, **LH/FSH**
  - **TSH**
  - **Fasting glucose or HbA1c**
  - **Fasting lipid panel**
  - Consider **prolactin** if low libido/low testosterone or symptoms suggest pituitary issue
  - Optional baseline **CMP** (renal/hepatic function) prior to ongoing medication use

### Treatment
- **PDE5 inhibitor trial (tadalafil/Cialis)** after counseling and contraindication review:
  - **Tadalafil 10 mg PO** at least 30–60 minutes before sexual activity **as needed**; may increase to **20 mg PRN** if inadequate response and tolerated, or decrease to 5 mg if side effects.
  - **Max 1 dose per 24 hours.**
  - Counsel: requires sexual stimulation; avoid excessive alcohol; common side effects include headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, back pain.
  - **Contraindications/precautions**: absolutely avoid **nitrates**; caution with alpha-blockers; seek urgent care for chest pain, priapism (>4 hours), sudden vision/hearing loss.
- If primary issue is actually **premature ejaculation**, discuss behavioral techniques (stop-start/squeeze), condoms, and consider SSRI options at follow-up if confirmed.

### Lifestyle / risk factor modification
- **Sleep/shift-work**: optimize sleep schedule; fatigue can worsen erectile function.
- Regular exercise, weight management, limit alcohol, avoid recreational drugs.
- Discuss cardiovascular risk: ED can precede cardiometabolic disease even in young men.

### Blood pressure
- **Recheck BP** (repeat in clinic or home BP log: 2 readings AM/PM for 1–2 weeks).
- Counsel on sodium reduction, exercise, weight management.
- If persistently ≥130/80 (or DBP ≥80) on repeat readings, address formally with diagnosis/risk stratification.

### Follow-up
- **Follow up in 4–6 weeks** to review symptom response, side effects, BP trend, and lab results.
- **Earlier follow-up** if medication not tolerated or symptoms rapidly worsen.
- **Referral**: consider **Urology** if inadequate response to PDE5 inhibitor after dose optimization and confirmed proper use, abnormal hormonal work-up, penile curvature/pain, or concern for organic pathology. Consider **behavioral health/sex therapy** if significant performance anxiety, depression/anxiety, or relationship factors emerge.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **COPD/emphysema, clinically stable (chronic dyspnea on exertion)**
   - Symptoms and exam are consistent with chronic COPD (decreased breath sounds, distant heart tones, mild cough/sputum), without features of acute exacerbation today (no fever/chills, no increased sputum volume/purulence reported, no chest pain).  
   - **Resting room-air SpO₂ 90%** suggests at least moderate resting hypoxemia and warrants assessment for need for long-term oxygen therapy and exertional/nocturnal desaturation.

2. **Chronic hypoxemia—borderline at rest**
   - SpO₂ 90% is low and may correspond to PaO₂ near threshold where oxygen is indicated, especially if lower with exertion or sleep or if evidence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale/polycythemia.

3. **Rhinitis/upper airway inflammation**
   - Mild–moderate nasal mucosal erythema/edema; may contribute to cough/postnasal drip.

4. **Psychiatric illness (agitated depression) with significant psychosocial stressors / placement concerns**
   - Recently hospitalized for psychiatric reasons and currently in a nursing facility; distressed about living situation. This affects adherence, functional capacity, and safety planning.

---

## PLAN
### 1) COPD / Emphysema
- **Continue current COPD regimen** as currently prescribed (per nursing facility MAR/med list); no change today given stable symptoms and exam.
- **Assess COPD control and optimize inhaler technique**
  - Review current inhalers/nebulizers, dosing schedule, and adherence with nursing staff.
  - Confirm proper technique and spacer use if applicable.
- **Pulmonary function testing**
  - Order **spirometry with bronchodilator** (and full PFTs with DLCO if available) to reassess severity since last pulmonary clinic visit (not seen since 2004).
- **Vaccinations**
  - Ensure **influenza annually** and **pneumococcal vaccination** up to date per current guidelines; administer if not current at facility.
- **Pulmonary rehabilitation / activity**
  - If feasible through the facility: **referral to pulmonary rehab** or structured exercise/conditioning program; reinforce pacing and energy conservation.
- **Exacerbation action plan**
  - Educate patient and nursing staff on warning signs (increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume/purulence, fever) and when to contact clinic/seek urgent care.

### 2) Hypoxemia / Oxygen needs
- **Objective assessment**
  - Order **arterial blood gas (ABG) on room air** to document PaO₂/PaCO₂ and evaluate for chronic hypercapnia.
  - Order **6-minute walk test with continuous oximetry** (or standardized exertional oximetry at facility) to assess exertional desaturation and oxygen requirement with activity.
  - Consider **overnight oximetry** if symptoms/history suggest sleep-related desaturation.
- **Oxygen therapy**
  - If ABG shows **PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SpO₂ ≤88%** at rest, or meets criteria with comorbidities (pulmonary HTN/cor pulmonale/polycythemia), initiate/continue **long-term oxygen therapy** per protocol.
  - If desaturates with exertion, prescribe **ambulatory oxygen** titrated to maintain SpO₂ ≥90% during activity.

### 3) Rhinitis / postnasal drip
- Start **intranasal corticosteroid** (e.g., fluticasone 1–2 sprays each nostril daily) if not already on one.
- Saline nasal spray/irrigation PRN.
- Avoid macrolides for future infections given **erythromycin allergy**; clarify nature of reaction in chart.

### 4) Psychiatric/placement concerns
- Coordinate with facility team:
  - **Communicate with psychiatry/primary team/social work** regarding patient’s distress, goals of care, and capacity/safety evaluation for independent living.
  - Encourage continued psychiatric follow-up and medication adherence.
- Consider **case management** involvement to address functional status, support services, and realistic discharge planning.

### 5) Follow-up
- **Return to Pulmonary Clinic in 3 months** (sooner if worsening dyspnea, increased sputum, fever, or new oxygen requirement).
- Review PFTs, ABG, and exertional/overnight oximetry results at follow-up to finalize oxygen plan and consider inhaler regimen adjustments based on severity and exacerbation history.

llm_plan:
## ASSESSMENT
1. **Daytime hypersomnolence/fatigue with sleep fragmentation — PSG negative for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)**
   - Full-night PSG shows **AHI < 1/hr**, stable oxygenation (low–mid 90s), and **no periodic limb movements**, arguing strongly **against clinically significant OSA** or PLMD as the cause of her symptoms.
   - She has **very short sleep latency (< 1 minute)** in the lab, consistent with **marked physiologic sleepiness**, likely from a combination of **insufficient/poor-quality sleep at home**, **sedating medications**, depression, and deconditioning.

2. **Snoring with intermittent inspiratory flow limitation (possible upper-airway resistance / primary snoring)**
   - PSG documented **intermittent inspiratory flow limitation compatible with snoring** without frank apneas/hypopneas. This can still contribute to perceived sleep disruption in some patients, particularly with nasal obstruction.

3. **Chronic insomnia (sleep initiation and maintenance)**
   - Reports difficulty falling asleep and recurrent awakenings every 1–2 hours at home; sleep was better in the lab. Pattern is most consistent with **psychophysiologic/behavioral insomnia**, potentially worsened by **late-evening nicotine**, psychiatric comorbidity, and medication effects.

4. **Absent REM sleep on PSG**
   - Likely medication-related (**high-dose SSRI/Paxil**, trazodone, quetiapine) and/or first-night/lab effects. Not, by itself, diagnostic, but may contribute to non-restorative sleep.

5. **Nasal obstruction/rhinitis with deviated septum and mucosal edema; intermittent epistaxis**
   - Exam shows septal deviation, mucosal edema, and bloody exudate; may worsen snoring/flow limitation and sleep quality.

6. **Tobacco use disorder, heavy (1–2 PPD)**
   - Likely contributing to insomnia (stimulant effect, especially if smoking after dinner), airway inflammation, and overall fatigue.

7. **Obesity with mild restrictive ventilatory defect on PFTs; exertional dyspnea/deconditioning**
   - Restriction with preserved DLCO is compatible with obesity-related restriction; daytime oxygenation is normal.

8. **Mild lower-extremity edema**
   - 1+ pretibial edema; needs PCP evaluation to exclude medication effect, venous insufficiency, cardiac/renal/hepatic contributors (given HTN and hepatitis C history).

---

## PLAN
1. **Sleep-disordered breathing / snoring**
   - Reviewed PSG results: **no indication for CPAP/BiPAP** at this time given **no significant OSA** and no desaturation.
   - **Conservative measures**:
     - Continue **weight loss** efforts (already down ~30 lb; encourage ongoing gradual loss).
     - **Positional strategies** (avoid supine sleep if it worsens snoring).
     - Optimize **nasal patency** (see rhinitis plan below).
   - If symptoms worsen (witnessed apneas, gasping/choking returns, weight gain, worsening sleepiness), consider **repeat PSG** (or home sleep test) to reassess.

2. **Excessive daytime sleepiness / safety**
   - Counsel on **drowsy driving** and high-risk activities; avoid driving if sleepy.

1. **Resistant / refractory hypertension – improved control with improved adherence, but still above goal systolic today (157/56) with low diastolic pressure.**  
   On 5 antihypertensive agents (ARB, CCB, beta-blocker, thiazide/K-sparing diuretic, alpha-blocker). She is asymptomatic and appears euvolemic on exam. The **wide pulse pressure and low DBP (56)** suggest **isolated systolic HTN of aging**; we should be cautious about overly aggressive lowering of DBP given coronary perfusion concerns in the elderly. Need to confirm control with home/ambulatory readings and review renal function/electrolytes given ARB + triamterene.

2. **Bradycardia (HR 47) in the setting of atenolol and history of AV block with pacemaker.**  
   She denies dizziness, syncope, or exercise intolerance beyond baseline. Nonetheless HR is quite low; medication effect and/or pacemaker programming should be reviewed to ensure adequate chronotropic support and to avoid unnecessary beta-blocker dosing.

3. **History of AV block with pacemaker / history of arrhythmia.**  
   Clinically stable today without cardiopulmonary symptoms, but needs routine device/cardiology follow-up and rhythm assessment given bradycardia.

4. **Right buttock pain, likely musculoskeletal/lumbosacral etiology (possible radicular pain/sciatica).**  
   No red flag symptoms documented (no weakness, no progressive neurologic deficits, no systemic symptoms). Needs conservative management and PCP follow-up; avoid NSAIDs given prior GI bleed and age.

5. **Remote GI bleed (1995).**  
   Important for analgesic choices and if future antiplatelet/anticoagulant considerations arise.

6. **History of depression.**  
   Not addressed in detail today; no acute concerns raised.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Hypertension (resistant; improved but not at goal)
- **Continue current antihypertensive regimen for now** given improved adherence and absence of symptoms, with caution about further lowering diastolic BP:
  - Triamterene/HCTZ 37.5/25 mg daily  
  - Amlodipine (Norvasc) 10 mg daily  
  - Candesartan (Atacand) 32 mg daily  
  - Doxazosin (Cardura) 4 mg daily  
  - Atenolol 50 mg daily (see bradycardia plan below)
- **Confirm true BP control:**
  - Review technique; repeat manual BP if available and check **orthostatic vitals** next visit (and sooner if dizziness).
  - **Home BP log**: twice daily readings (AM/PM) for 1–2 weeks; bring cuff to next visit to validate.
  - Consider **ambulatory BP monitoring** if home vs clinic readings are discordant (evaluate white-coat effect).
- **Lifestyle:** reinforce **low-sodium diet**, avoid excess NSAIDs/decongestants, maintain activity as tolerated.

**Labs (safety/secondary contributors):**
- **BMP/CMP** (Na, K, CO₂, BUN/Cr/eGFR, glucose) given ARB + K-sparing diuretic.
- **Urinalysis + urine albumin/creatinine ratio** to assess kidney involvement/target organ effects.
- **CBC** (baseline, anemia considerations in elderly; also given remote GI bleed history).
- Additional labs (TSH, renin/aldosterone) only if clinically indicated based on results/trajectory (not urgent today given improved trend).

**Medication optimization (to revisit after data):**
- If home systolic BP remains persistently elevated and labs allow, consider a **more evidence-based resistant HTN strategy** (e.g., adjusting diuretic to a longer-acting thiazide-like agent and/or adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist), but this must be weighed against **low DBP** and risk of hyperkalemia on current regimen.

### 2) Bradycardia (HR 47) / pacemaker

- **Cardiology/electrophysiology follow-up for pacemaker interrogation** and rate settings given low HR; ensure appropriate lower rate limit and percent pacing.
- **Review need for atenolol dose**:
  - If cardiology agrees and there is no compelling indication for the current dose (e.g., active tachyarrhythmia control), consider **dose reduction** (e.g., 25 mg daily) or alternative strategy to avoid excessive bradycardia.  
  - Patient instructed to seek care urgently for **syncope, near-syncope, new dizziness, chest pain, or shortness of breath**.

### 3) Musculoskeletal right buttock pain
- **Conservative measures:** heat/ice, gentle stretching/physical activity as tolerated.
- **Analgesia:** prefer **acetaminophen** as needed (within safe dosing limits); **avoid NSAIDs** if possible given age, hypertension, and prior GI bleed.
- **Referral/Follow-up:** advise follow-up with **primary care**; consider **physical therapy** if persistent. Imaging (lumbar spine/hip) only if symptoms persist/worsen or if neurologic deficits/red flags develop.

### 4) Depression history
- Screen at next PCP visit or nephrology follow-up if concerns arise; ensure continuity of mental health care/medications if applicable.

---

- **Renal/HTN clinic follow-up in ~3–4 months**, sooner if home BPs are persistently high (e.g., SBP >170 repeatedly) or if symptomatic hypotension/bradycardia occurs.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **ADHD – good response to stimulant with inadequate duration of coverage (AM “lag” + afternoon rebound).**  
   Child started **Adderall XR 10 mg daily** last month with **marked improvement** reported by parent/teachers and clear worsening when a dose was missed—supporting ADHD diagnosis and medication effectiveness. Current concerns suggest **delayed onset in the morning** and **wearing off by ~2 PM** with evening behavioral difficulty, consistent with **insufficient duration** for full school/day coverage.  
2. **Appetite/weight change likely related to stimulant.**  
   Weight decreased from **49 lb to 46.5 lb** over the past month. Appetite suppression initially noted but now improving; still requires monitoring given young age and stimulant use.

---

## PLAN
### 1) ADHD medication management
- **Adjust medication for longer coverage:**
  - **Increase Adderall XR to 15 mg PO each morning** (age/weight-appropriate next titration step given strong benefit but short duration).  
  - Discussed that XR typically lasts longer, but some children metabolize faster; dose titration is appropriate when benefit is clear and side effects are acceptable.
- **Alternative/next step if still wearing off early or if side effects increase:** consider **adding a small short-acting stimulant “booster” dose early afternoon** (to be taken at school) *or* switch to a different long-acting formulation (e.g., lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate ER). Will reassess at follow-up before adding booster.
- **Administration counseling:** take as early as feasible in the morning; keep consistent timing daily. Avoid taking late morning/afternoon to reduce insomnia risk.

### 2) Growth/appetite and side-effect monitoring
- Encourage **high-calorie/protein breakfast before or with medication**, calorie-dense after-school snack, and good dinner when medication effect wanes.
- Monitor for stimulant adverse effects: **decreased appetite/weight loss, insomnia, headaches, stomachaches, irritability, mood changes, tics, palpitations/chest pain**. Family to call promptly if significant.

### 3) Monitoring / vitals
- At next visit: obtain **BP/HR**, full height/weight and plot growth curve. (Physical exam deferred today, but needs routine monitoring while on stimulants.)
- No labs/imaging indicated at this time based on current history.

### 4) School/behavioral supports
- Continue school collaboration; recommend parent request teacher feedback using a simple rating scale (e.g., **Vanderbilt follow-up** form) after dose adjustment to document benefits and any rebound.

### 5) Follow-up
- **Follow up in 3–4 weeks** to reassess symptom control across the day, appetite/weight trend, sleep, and teacher reports; sooner for adverse effects or if symptoms worsen.
- Provide refill plan consistent with controlled-substance prescribing; no early refills for lost medication; store securely.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Interstitial lung disease secondary to lupus pneumonitis – clinically stable.**  
   Doing well since last visit with **no cough, sputum, fevers, or exertional dyspnea**. **Resting/ambulatory O2 sat 94–96% on room air**. CXR today shows **mild interstitial markings** consistent with known history and appears **not worse** compared with prior CT description (no prior CXR available for direct comparison). She recently stopped low-dose prednisone (2.5 mg) on 6/16/04 without clear pulmonary decline.

2. **New back/joint pain with discomfort on deep inspiration – likely musculoskeletal vs lupus flare/serositis; low suspicion for acute pulmonary infection today.**  
   Symptoms began yesterday, no infectious symptoms, exam without focal findings, O2 normal. Pleuritic-type discomfort could be musculoskeletal from flare/arthritis or lupus pleuritis; will coordinate with Rheumatology and monitor closely for evolution.

3. **Fatigue – nonspecific; consider lupus activity, anemia/cytopenias from Imuran, thyroid status, etc.**  
   Given systemic symptoms and immunosuppression, labs are appropriate.

4. **Rhinitis/nasal inflammation on exam.**  
   Mild–moderate erythema/edema; may contribute to upper airway symptoms though she denies cough presently.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Lupus pneumonitis / ILD monitoring
- **Continue current pulmonary regimen**: Advair 1 puff BID (as currently prescribed) unless adverse effects.
- **Pulmonary function testing (PFTs)**: order **spirometry, lung volumes, and DLCO** to establish current baseline and trend given long interval since last pulmonary visit.
- **Imaging**:
  - Request/obtain **prior chest imaging** (outside CXR if any; prior CT images/report) for direct comparison.
  - **No urgent CT** today given clinical stability; **consider HRCT chest** if PFTs worsen, symptoms increase, or if comparison suggests progression.
- **Oxygen**: none indicated now. Continue routine activity as tolerated; call if new exertional desaturation, dyspnea, or cough.

### 2) Back/joint pain with pleuritic discomfort (possible lupus flare vs MSK)
- **Coordinate with Rheumatology** (message/call today): review symptoms in context of recent prednisone discontinuation and current Imuran/Plaquenil dosing; consider whether this represents inflammatory flare and whether steroid bridge is needed (decision deferred to Rheumatology/primary lupus management team).
- **Evaluate for complications/red flags**:
  - If she develops **worsening pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, fever, asymmetric leg swelling**, or sustained O2 sat <92%, she should seek urgent evaluation to rule out PE/pneumonia/pleuritis.
- **Symptomatic treatment**: may use **acetaminophen** as needed (within safe daily limits). Avoid NSAIDs if contraindicated by her lupus/renal/GI history (not fully known here); if she typically tolerates NSAIDs and has no contraindications, Rheumatology/PCP may advise.

### 3) Fatigue / medication monitoring (Imuran + lupus activity)
- **Labs (coordinate with Rheumatology/PCP, but reasonable to obtain now):**
  - **CBC with differential** (cytopenias)
  - **CMP/LFTs** (Imuran monitoring; renal function)
  - **ESR/CRP**
  - **Urinalysis + urine protein/creatinine ratio** (screen for lupus nephritis contributing to fatigue)
  - **Complement C3/C4 and anti-dsDNA** (lupus activity)
  - **TSH/free T4** (on Synthroid; fatigue)
- Review results with Rheumatology and adjust immunosuppression as appropriate.

### 4) Rhinitis
- Start **intranasal corticosteroid** (e.g., fluticasone 1–2 sprays each nostril daily) and/or saline irrigation as needed.
- Reassess if she develops chronic cough, sinus symptoms, or recurrent infections.

### 5) Preventive / safety counseling (immunosuppressed)
- Ensure **influenza vaccine annually** and **pneumococcal vaccination** per guidelines (coordinate with PCP).
- Reinforce infection precautions and to report fevers promptly.

### FOLLOW-UP
- **Pulmonary follow-up in ~6 months** (or sooner if symptoms recur), ideally with **PFTs completed beforehand**.  
- **Earlier follow-up (within days–weeks)** if pleuritic pain persists/worsens, new respiratory symptoms develop, or labs suggest increased lupus activity or medication toxicity.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Right plantar fasciitis (most likely)**  
   - 2-week history of heel pain **worst with first step in the morning** and worsened with activity, with **point tenderness at the medial tubercle of the calcaneus** and pain extending into the **medial arch**. No signs of infection, no neurovascular compromise, and no systemic symptoms. Presentation is classic for plantar fasciitis.

2. **Right heel pain – rule out alternate etiologies if not improving** (less likely at this time)  
   - Differential includes calcaneal stress fracture, nerve entrapment (e.g., Baxter’s nerve), fat pad contusion/atrophy, inflammatory arthropathy. Current exam and story most consistent with plantar fasciitis; no red flags reported, but will reassess if refractory.

---

## PLAN
### Conservative treatment (first-line)
- **Activity modification:** Reduce high-impact activity and prolonged standing/walking as able for the next 2–4 weeks; gradual return as symptoms improve.
- **Stretching program (daily):**
  - Plantar fascia-specific stretch (dorsiflex toes, hold 30 sec) and **calf/Achilles stretches** (3–5 sets, 2–3x/day).
  - Strengthening: intrinsic foot exercises as tolerated.
- **Ice:** Roll foot over frozen water bottle or ice massage to plantar heel **10–15 min** after activity and/or 1–2x/day.
- **Supportive footwear:** Avoid barefoot/flat slippers; use supportive shoes with firm heel counter and arch support.
- **Orthotics:** Start with **OTC arch supports/heel cups**; consider custom orthotics if persistent.
- **Night splint:** Consider if significant morning pain persists after initial measures.

### Medications / symptom control
- **NSAID trial if no contraindications:** e.g., **ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO q6–8h PRN pain** with food for up to 1–2 weeks, or **naproxen 220 mg PO BID PRN**.  
  - Review/avoid if history of ulcer/GI bleed, kidney disease, anticoagulation, uncontrolled HTN, etc.
- Alternative/adjunct: **topical diclofenac gel** to plantar heel PRN.

### Imaging / tests
- **No imaging today** given typical presentation and short duration.
- **Obtain weight-bearing foot X-rays** if:
  - pain persists beyond **6–8 weeks** despite appropriate conservative care,
  - atypical features develop (rest/night pain, significant swelling, focal bony tenderness),
  - concern for stress fracture or other pathology.

### Procedures (if refractory)
- If not improving after **6–8+ weeks** of consistent conservative therapy: discuss
  - **corticosteroid injection** (benefits/risks reviewed: plantar fascia rupture, fat pad atrophy),
  - formal **physical therapy**,
  - other options per course (e.g., immobilization boot for severe symptoms, ESWT depending on availability).

### Patient education / precautions
- Expect gradual improvement; many cases take **6–12 weeks** with consistent therapy.
- Return sooner for **worsening pain**, inability to bear weight, new swelling/bruising, numbness/tingling, or systemic symptoms.

### Follow-up
- **Follow up in 4–6 weeks** to reassess pain/function and adherence to stretching/footwear/orthotic plan; sooner PRN.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Polycythemia vera (JAK2+) with secondary/post-PV myelofibrosis**  
   - Long-standing PV (dx ~2005/2006) with evolution to secondary myelofibrosis, prior intolerance to hydroxyurea, interferon, and later lenalidomide (fatigue/diarrhea). Not a transplant candidate (no sibling donor; MUD deemed not feasible due to support and relatively stable status).  
   - Today with **marked leukocytosis (WBC 41.9k, ANC 34.4k)** and **palpable splenomegaly (~4 FB below LCM)**. Platelets are preserved (235k) and hemoglobin 14.8. Recent short course of steroids could contribute to neutrophilia, but degree is significant and warrants trending and assessment for progression/inflammation/infection.

2. **Severe microcytosis (MCV 56.7) with normal hemoglobin**  
   - Marked microcytosis is most consistent with **iron deficiency** (often from prior phlebotomy and/or chronic blood loss), though thalassemia trait is also on the differential. Needs iron studies before any supplementation decision (iron replacement can increase erythrocytosis in PV).

3. **Left shin pain after recent trauma; swelling resolved**  
   - Exam: mild tibial tenderness without deformity; no current edema. Concern for **contusion/stress injury**; fracture less likely but should be ruled out if focal bony pain persists. DVT appears unlikely now given resolution of swelling and lack of edema, but patient has underlying MPN-associated thrombosis risk—low threshold to image if swelling returns.

4. **Thrombosis risk in MPN / cardiovascular risk factors**  
   - MPN increases arterial/venous thrombosis risk. Ensure antiplatelet therapy and risk-factor modification as appropriate.

5. **Marijuana use**  
   - Using for appetite/weight gain; counsel re risks (cognition, dependence, smoke exposure) and discuss safer routes if continuing.

---

## PLAN
### 1) PV with secondary myelofibrosis / leukocytosis / splenomegaly
- **Repeat/confirm labs and evaluate for contributing causes**
  - **CBC with differential** in **1–2 weeks** to trend leukocytosis after steroid exposure resolves.
  - **CMP**, **LDH**, **uric acid**, and **peripheral smear** (left shift/blasts/dysplasia).
  - Assess for occult infection/inflammation based on symptoms; if any fever, cough, urinary symptoms, etc., add targeted workup (e.g., UA/culture, CXR).
- **Disease status reassessment**
  - If leukocytosis persists/increases, new cytopenias develop, splenomegaly worsens, or constitutional symptoms increase (night sweats, fevers, weight loss, early satiety), recommend **repeat bone marrow biopsy/aspirate** with cytogenetics/NGS to reassess myelofibrosis status and rule out acceleration.
- **Therapy discussion (given prior intolerance to HU/IFN/lenalidomide)**
  - If symptomatic splenomegaly, progressive leukocytosis, or worsening MF symptoms: discuss starting a **JAK inhibitor (e.g., ruxolitinib)** if blood counts and clinical profile allow; review risks (cytopenias, infections, zoster reactivation) and monitoring plan.
  - Continue supportive care if clinically stable and patient prefers observation.
- **Thrombosis prophylaxis**
  - If no contraindication (history of major bleeding, active GI bleeding, aspirin allergy): continue/initiate **low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily** (confirm current use in med list).
  - Reinforce hydration and prompt evaluation for thrombotic symptoms (new unilateral swelling/pain, chest pain, dyspnea, neuro deficits).

### 2) Microcytosis / possible iron deficiency
- Order **iron studies**: ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; consider **reticulocyte count**.
- If iron deficient:
  - Do **not** empirically replace iron without a plan, given PV physiology; decision based on symptoms, hemoglobin trend, and thrombosis/erythrocytosis risk.
  - If iron deficiency confirmed, evaluate source if not clearly attributable to past phlebotomy: **FIT/FOBT** and/or coordinate with PCP/GI for age-appropriate colon cancer screening and GI evaluation as indicated.

### 3) Left shin pain after injury
- **Imaging:** Order **X-ray of the left tibia/fibula** to rule out fracture/stress injury given focal bony tenderness.
- **Symptom control:** Acetaminophen as needed (avoid exceeding 3,000 mg/day; avoid NSAIDs if any bleeding risk/renal disease—none evident today).
- **Return precautions:** If swelling recurs, pain worsens, redness/warmth develops, or new calf swelling/shortness of breath occurs → urgent evaluation; low threshold for **venous duplex ultrasound** due to MPN-related clot risk.

### 4) Health maintenance / risk modification
- Encourage **avoidance of tobacco smoke exposure**; discuss marijuana risks and consider non-smoked routes if continuing.
- Blood pressure today mildly elevated (144/85): advise follow-up with PCP for BP management.

### 5) Follow-up
- **Follow up in hematology clinic in 4–6 weeks** (earlier if worsening symptoms), with interim **CBC in 1–2 weeks**.
- Review imaging results (tibia/fibula X-ray) when available and adjust plan accordingly.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 8) s/p prostate fossa irradiation for recurrence, now with rising PSA (PSA 1.2 and slowly increasing over recent months)**  
   - At ~21 months post–salvage RT, a continued PSA rise is concerning for **biochemical progression** and possible **metastatic or locoregional disease**. Needs restaging to guide next management (observation vs systemic therapy and/or metastasis-directed therapy).

2. **Acute onset urinary frequency/nocturia with abdominal cramping x 2 days**  
   - Abrupt symptom onset favors **infectious/irritative cystitis (UTI)** or **acute bladder irritation** (possibly related to viral illness/dehydration/caffeine, etc.) more than late radiation cystitis, though prior pelvic RT remains a risk factor. Needs urinalysis/culture and evaluation for retention.

3. **Erectile dysfunction (treatment-related), libido intact**  
   - Consistent with post-treatment sexual dysfunction.

4. **Intermittent hemorrhoidal irritation; no hematochezia**  
   - Stable; no alarm features reported today.

5. **Sore throat/URI symptoms with household exposure**  
   - Likely viral.

---

## PLAN
### 1) Rising PSA after salvage RT (concern for biochemical progression)
- **Labs**
  - **Repeat PSA** to confirm trajectory (repeat in **4–6 weeks** or sooner if oncology prefers).
  - **Total testosterone** (baseline prior to any androgen deprivation therapy consideration).
  - **CBC, CMP** (baseline prior to potential systemic therapy; assess renal/hepatic function).
- **Imaging / Restaging**
  - Order **PSMA PET/CT** (preferred given PSA 1.2 and rising) to localize disease (local vs nodal vs distant).
  - If PSMA PET not available/covered: **CT abdomen/pelvis + bone scan** as alternative.
- **Referrals**
  - **Medical Oncology and/or Urology**: discuss management options for biochemical progression after salvage RT, including:
    - **Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)** timing (intermittent vs continuous depending on imaging/PSA kinetics and patient goals)
    - Consideration of **metastasis-directed therapy** if oligometastatic disease on PSMA PET
    - Clinical trial options if appropriate
- **Follow-up**
  - Review imaging and PSA trend with patient promptly after results (typically **within 2–4 weeks** once completed).

### 2) Acute urinary frequency/nocturia and cramping
- **Tests today**
  - **Urinalysis with microscopy and urine culture**
  - **Post-void residual (PVR)** bladder scan if available (evaluate for retention/overflow or obstruction)
- **Symptomatic management (while awaiting results)**
  - Encourage **hydration**; avoid bladder irritants (**caffeine, alcohol, spicy/citrus**) for the next week.
  - If significant bothersome nocturia/urgency and no contraindications, start **tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO nightly** (counsel dizziness/orthostasis).
- **If UA/culture supports UTI**
  - Treat with culture-directed antibiotic; if empiric treatment is needed based on symptoms/UA while pending culture, choose antibiotic based on allergies, renal function, and local resistance patterns (e.g., **nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID x 5 days** for uncomplicated cystitis if appropriate; avoid if concern for pyelonephritis).
- **If UA negative and symptoms persist >1–2 weeks**
  - Consider **overactive bladder** therapy (e.g., **mirabegron** or antimuscarinic depending on PVR and contraindications).
  - Consider **urology evaluation/cystoscopy** especially if any **hematuria**, recurrent symptoms, or concern for **radiation cystitis/stricture**.
- **Return/ER precautions**
  - Fever/chills, flank pain, vomiting, inability to urinate, worsening abdominal pain, or **gross hematuria**.

### 3) Erectile dysfunction
- Discuss options; patient preference-driven:
  - Trial **PDE5 inhibitor** (e.g., **sildenafil 50 mg** 30–60 minutes before sexual activity; may titrate to 100 mg as tolerated; avoid with nitrates).
  - Consider **vacuum erection device** and/or **referral to Men’s Health/Urology** for injections or other therapies if desired.

### 4) Hemorrhoids/rectal irritation (stable)
- Conservative care: **fiber supplementation**, adequate fluids, avoid straining, **sitz baths**.
- If flare: short course topical therapy (e.g., **hydrocortisone rectal cream/suppository** as needed).
- If any new bleeding, anemia symptoms, or persistent worsening: consider **GI/colorectal** evaluation.

### 5) Sore throat/URI symptoms
- Supportive care (fluids, acetaminophen/NSAIDs if safe).
- Consider **COVID/flu testing** based on local prevalence/symptom course and risk factors.
- Seek care if high fever, shortness of breath, severe/persistent symptoms, or dehydration.

**Follow-up:**  
- **Sooner (within days)** if urinary symptoms worsen or systemic symptoms develop; otherwise **2–4 weeks** to review UA/culture response and ensure restaging/imaging plans are in progress, and to coordinate oncology/urology next steps.

## ASSESSMENT
1. **Left posterior shoulder erythema with lymphangitic streaking – most consistent with early cellulitis/lymphangitis likely secondary to an insect bite**  
   - 6 cm area of faint erythema with a central punctum, minimal tenderness, and **erythematous streaks tracking toward the neck** suggests **lymphangitis** from a superficial skin infection.  
   - No fever, no necrosis/eschar, and no significant pain makes serious spider envenomation (e.g., brown recluse) less likely at this time, though the inciting event may have been an insect/spider bite.

## PLAN
### 1) Treat presumed cellulitis/lymphangitis
- **Start oral antibiotics with streptococcal and MSSA coverage:**
  - **Cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h x 7 days** (adjust duration based on response; may stop at 5 days if rapid and near-complete resolution, otherwise complete 7–10 days).
  - If significant penicillin/cephalosporin allergy: **Clindamycin 300 mg PO q6–8h x 7 days**.
- **Supportive care**
  - Warm compresses to the area **10–15 min, 3–4x/day**.
  - Keep area clean/dry; avoid scratching.
  - **Acetaminophen or ibuprofen PRN** for discomfort (use NSAIDs cautiously if any kidney issues; patient is on Maxzide).
- **Mark and monitor**
  - Outline border of redness with a pen today to monitor spread.

### 2) Evaluate for abscess/necrosis and progression
- No fluctuance noted today; **no drainage procedure indicated**.
- If the area becomes more painful, develops a “head,” fluctuance, drainage, or rapid enlargement, return for **re-exam and possible incision and drainage** and/or broadened antibiotic coverage.

### 3) Labs/Imaging
- **No labs or imaging needed today** given absence of fever/systemic symptoms and mild exam.
- If worsening, systemic symptoms, immunocompromise, or failure to improve in 48 hours: consider **CBC** and **consider ultrasound** of the area to assess for occult abscess.

### 4) Safety/return precautions (urgent)
Go to urgent care/ED or contact clinic immediately for:
- Fever/chills, rapid spread beyond the marked border, increasing pain, swelling, or new drainage
- Development of black/blue discoloration, blistering, necrosis, or severe tenderness
- Red streaking progressing significantly, enlarged/painful lymph nodes, or feeling ill
- Any facial/neck swelling, difficulty swallowing/breathing

### 5) Follow-up
- **Recheck in 24–48 hours** (in clinic or sooner if worsening) to confirm improvement given lymphangitic streaking and location near the neck.
- If improving, complete antibiotics and follow up as needed until resolved.

The patient at that time stated that he had established diagnosis of liver cirrhosis.  Since the last visit the patient was asked to sign a lease of information form and we sent request for information from the doctor the patient saw before, Dr. X in Las Cruces and his primary care physician in Silver City, and unfortunately we did not get any information from anybody.  Also the patient had admission in Gila Medical Center with epigastric pain, diarrhea, and confusion.  He spent 3 days in the hospital.  He was followed by Dr. X and unfortunately we also do not have the information of what was wrong with the patient.  From the patient's report he was diagnosed with some kind of viral infection.  At the time of admission he had a lot of epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION,VITAL SIGNS:  Weight 107, height 6 feet 1 inch, blood pressure 128/67, heart rate 74, saturation 98%; pain is 3/10 with localization of the pain in the epigastric area.,HEENT:  PERRLA.  EOM intact.  Oropharynx is clear of lesions.,NECK:  Supple.  No lymphadenopathy.  No thyromegaly.,LUNGS:  Clear to auscultation and percussion bilateral.,CARDIOVASCULAR:  Regular rate and rhythm.  No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.,ABDOMEN:  Not tender, not distended.  Splenomegaly about 4 cm under the costal margin.  No hepatomegaly.  Bowel sounds present.,MUSCULOSKELETAL:  No cyanosis, no clubbing, no pitting edema.,NEUROLOGIC:  Nonfocal.  No asterixis.  No costovertebral tenderness.,PSYCHE:  The patient is oriented x4, alert and cooperative.,LABORATORY DATA: , We were able to collect lab results from Medical Center; we got only CMP from the hospital which showed glucose level 79, BUN 9, creatinine 0.6, sodium 136, potassium 3.5, chloride 104, CO2 23.7, calcium 7.3, total protein 5.9, albumin 2.5, total bilirubin 5.63.  His AST 56, ALT 37, alkaline phosphatase 165, and his ammonia level was 53.  We do not have any other results back.  No hepatitis panels.  No alpha-fetoprotein level. The patient had chronic pain syndrome, he had multiple back surgeries, and he has taken opiate for a prolonged period of time.  In the office twice the patient did not have any abdominal pain on physical exam.  His pain does not sound like obstruction of common bile duct and he had these episodes of abdominal pain almost continuously.  He probably requires increased level of pain control with increased dose of opiates, which should be addressed with his primary care physician.,2.  End-stage liver disease.  Of course, we need to find out the cause of the liver cirrhosis.  We do not have hepatitis panel yet and we do not have information about the liver biopsy which was performed before.  We do not have any information of any type of investigation in the past.  Again, patient was seen by gastroenterologist already in Las Cruces, Dr. X.  The patient was advised to contact Dr. X by himself to convince him to send available information because we already send release information form signed by the patient without any result.  It will be not reasonable to repeat unnecessary tests in that point in time.,We are waiting for the hepatitis panel and alpha-fetoprotein level.  We will also need to get information about ultrasound which was done in Gila Medical Center, but obviously no tumor was found on this exam of the liver.  We have to figure out hepatitis status for another reason if he needs vaccination against hepatitis A and B.  Until now we do not know exactly what the cause of the patient's end-stage liver disease is and my differential diagnosis probably is hepatitis C.  The patient denied any excessive alcohol intake, but I could not preclude alcohol-related liver cirrhosis also.  We will need to look for nuclear antibody if it is not done before.  PSC is extremely unlikely but possible.  Wilson disease also possible diagnosis but again, we first have to figure out if these tests were done for the patient or not.  Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency will be extremely unlikely because the patient has no lung problem.  On his end-stage liver disease we already know that he had low platelet count splenomegaly.  We know that his bilirubin is elevated and albumin is very low.  I suspect that at the time of admission to the hospital the patient presented with encephalopathy.  We do not know if INR was checked to look for coagulopathy.  The patient had an EGD in 2005 as well as colonoscopy in Silver City.  We have to have this result to evaluate if the patient had any varices and if he needs any intervention for that.,At this point in time, I recommended the patient to continue to take lactulose 50 mL 3 times daily.  The patient tolerated it well; no diarrhea at this point in time.  I also recommended for him to contact his primary care physician for increased dose of opiates for him.  As a primary prophylaxis of GI bleeding in patient with end-stage liver disease we will try to use Inderal.  The patient got a prescription for 10 mg pills.  He will take 10 mg twice daily and we will gradually increase his dose until his heart rate will drop to 25% from 75% to probably 60-58.  The patient was educated how to use Inderal and he was explained why we decided to use this medication.  The patient will hold this medication if he is orthostatic or bradycardic.,Again, the patient and his wife were advised to contact all offices they have seen before to get information about what tests were already done and if on the next visit in 2 weeks we still do not have any information we will need to repeat all these tests I mentioned above.,We also discussed nutrition issues.  The patient was provided information that his protein intake is supposed to be about 25 g per day.  He was advised not to over-eat protein and advised not to starve.
